newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivorian cocoa product exports near twice '96 level.
newsitem.headline: Ivorian cocoa product exports near twice '96 level.

text.p: Ivory Coast's semi-finished cocoa products and powder exports rose to 8,864 tonnes in January from 7,160 tonnes in December but the cumulative total was almost twice the 1995/96 level, official shipping data show.

Cumulative product and powder shipments in the first four months of the 1996/97 (Oct-Sept) season -- including shipments from October 1 to October 24 when the season opened late -- were 31,873 tonnes against 18,560 tonnes in the same period of 1995/96.
Ivory Coast's cocoa processing capacity has risen steadily since late 1995 in line with its policy of boosting volumes.
Product shipments from Abidjan in January totalled 7,101 tonnes, including 331 tonnes of powder, whereas San Pedro shipped 1,763 tonnes of cocoa products shown grouped together in one category.

Product exports in January 1995 were only 4,565 tonnes but new factory capacity was added afterwards in Abidjan. A completely new factory in San Pedro, Ivory Coast's second port, came on stream in late 1995.

The figures do not separate liquor, butter and cake shipments but figures for powder exports are given. Cumulative shipments stand at 2,177 tonnes this season against 1,404 in 1995/96 and 38 tonnes the year before.
Ivory Coast has four processing factories with capacity set to rise to around 180,000 tonnes of beans a year.
Ivorian Commodities minister Guy-Alain Gauze said at International Cocoa Organization (ICCO) talks in London this week that Ivory Coast planned to process 300,000 tonnes of cocoa in 1997.
Local industry sources said completion of new processing capacity is unlikely before the 1997/98 cocoa season (Oct-Sept).
Abidjan-based UNICAO is planning a 21,500 tonnes extension to raise its factory capacity to 86,000 tonnes by January 1998.
A spokesman said the new extension could be complete by October but was unlikely to go on stream until the new year.
UNICAO's only main rival Callebaut-Barry has three plants grinding up to 80,000 tonnes of beans a year.
Other firms planning three new plants are still in discussions but if they proceed total processing capacity would rise to a maximum of around 330,000 tonnes.
Local processing of beans is part of Ivory Coast's policy to add value to exports while taking low quality mid-crop (April-Sept) beans off the international market.
U.S.-based Cargill, in discussion with Ivorian exporter SICC, expects no progress with its plans, or a final decision on whether to proceed, for at least another three months, sources said.
